title: The 'poured molten gold' death legend
description: Cassius Dio (40.27.1-2) records a tradition that the Parthians poured molten gold down Crassus's throat after his death as a mockery of his legendary greed. This story is almost certainly apocryphal — a dramatic embellishment that postdates the event and reflects the moralizing theme of Crassus's avarice found in ancient sources. Plutarch (Crass. 31-33) does not mention this detail, which suggests it entered the tradition later. The story serves a literary purpose: poetic justice for a man defined by wealth.

title: Crassus as 'Richest Man in Rome' — a modern superlative
description: The characterization of Crassus as 'the richest man in Rome' or 'the richest man in history' is a modern interpretive label, not an ancient statistical ranking. Plutarch (Crass. 2.3-6) reports his wealth at 7,100 talents and describes his accumulation methods in moralizing terms. However, the Roman Republic had no formal wealth registry, and intergenerational aristocratic wealth was not fungible in the way modern net-worth calculations assume. Pompey, Lucullus, and others may have controlled comparable resources. Modern scholars (Ward 1977, Marshall 1976) caution against treating this as a verified superlative.

title: The 'First Triumvirate' as historiographical construction
description: The term 'First Triumvirate' is a modern historiographical label, not a Roman constitutional office. The alliance of 60 BCE between Crassus, Pompey, and Caesar was a private political arrangement (societas or amicitia), not a legally constituted magistracy. The later Second Triumvirate (43 BCE) was legally ratified by the Lex Titia, creating a formal contrast that historians retroactively applied. Ancient sources refer to the 'three-headed monster' (Cicero, Att. 2.9) or 'compact' but not as a 'triumvirate.' This must be marked as reception/historiographical convention in any claims about the alliance.
